Part 1

Concept

Software Architecture Basics — Software architecture is the set of structural decisions that shape how a system decomposes responsibilities, communicates, persists state, and survives change.

Architecture is not a diagram you draw once — it is the reasoning that connects business capabilities to deployable units, quality attributes (latency, availability, security), and team ownership. Netflix, Amazon, and large banks all document architecture decisions because the cost of reversing structural choices grows exponentially after production traffic arrives.

Mental Model

+-------------+     +-------------+     +-------------+
|  Business   | --> |  Logical    | --> |  Physical   |
|  capability |     |  components |     |  deployment |
+-------------+     +-------------+     +-------------+
        |                   |                   |
        v                   v                   v
   Domain language    APIs & events        Pods / regions

Key Terms

Term Definition
Quality attribute Measurable property such as availability, latency, or modifiability.
Architectural style Recurring structure — monolith, layered, microservices, event-driven.
Trade-off analysis Explicit comparison of competing goals; no design optimizes everything.
Deployable unit Artifact independently released to production (JAR, container, function).
Conway's Law System structure mirrors communication structure of the organization.

Why Architects Care

  • Software Architecture Basics shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How Software Architecture Basics evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
1960s–70s Mainframe batch systems Centralized processing; architecture implicit in ops
1980s–90s Client-server + 3-tier Explicit separation of UI, logic, data
2000s SOA + ESB era Service contracts via XML/SOAP; heavy integration middleware
2010s Cloud + microservices Small deployables, DevOps, container orchestration
2020s Platform engineering Golden paths, internal developer platforms, FinOps

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt Software Architecture Basics because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do we structure a growing system so teams can deliver safely without accidental coupling that turns every feature into a full-system release?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. Ivory-tower architecture disconnected from delivery teams
  2. Big upfront design that freezes before learning
  3. Diagram-only architecture with no enforceable boundaries
  4. Copying Netflix microservices at 10k users scale
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

Without explicit architecture, codebases accrete dependencies until no one can predict blast radius of a change. Architecture exists to make quality attributes and ownership negotiable upfront rather than discovered during outages.

Design Goals

Goal How Software Architecture Basics Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for Software Architecture Basics follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

+-------------+     +-------------+     +-------------+
|  Business   | --> |  Logical    | --> |  Physical   |
|  capability |     |  components |     |  deployment |
+-------------+     +-------------+     +-------------+
        |                   |                   |
        v                   v                   v
   Domain language    APIs & events        Pods / regions

Step-by-Step

  1. Identify business capabilities and quality goals
  2. Choose structural style and integration patterns
  3. Define boundaries, contracts, and data ownership
  4. Validate with prototypes and failure-mode analysis
  5. Document ADRs and evolve as constraints change

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges
Part 6

Failure Modes

When Software Architecture Basics is misapplied, these failures appear repeatedly:

  • Ivory-tower architecture disconnected from delivery teams
  • Big upfront design that freezes before learning
  • Diagram-only architecture with no enforceable boundaries
  • Copying Netflix microservices at 10k users scale

Incident Pattern

User request ──► missing timeout ──► thread pool exhaustion ──► cascading 503s
                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges
Part 7

Scale Considerations

Software Architecture Basics at Amazon/Netflix/Uber scale requires explicit capacity thinking:

  • Amazon splits ownership by two-pizza teams aligned to service boundaries
  • Uber's domain-oriented microservices map org structure to deployables
  • Architectural reviews gate new cross-domain dependencies at scale

Scale Checklist

Dimension Question to Answer
Throughput What RPS per instance before saturation?
Data growth Which store becomes the bottleneck first?
Fan-out How many downstream calls per request?
Multi-region What consistency trade-off is acceptable?
Part 8

Performance

Performance for Software Architecture Basics is dominated by integration cost, not local CPU:

  • Structure affects fan-out: microservices multiply network hops
  • Caching and read models often follow architectural partitioning
  • Early monoliths optimize local calls; distributed styles pay RTT tax
Factor Typical Impact Mitigation
Network hops +1–5 ms per sync call Cache, batch, async where safe
Serialization CPU on large payloads Schema evolution, compression
Connection pools Queueing under burst Pool sizing + backpressure
Part 9

Java Example

Representative Java illustrating Software Architecture Basics:

public final class OrderCapability {
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final PaymentPort payments;

    public OrderCapability(OrderRepository orders, PaymentPort payments) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.payments = payments;
    }

    public OrderId place(OrderDraft draft) {
        Order order = orders.save(draft.toPendingOrder());
        payments.authorize(order.id(), draft.amount());
        return order.id();
    }
}

Reading the Example

  • Notice explicit boundaries — domain code does not reach into foreign persistence.
  • Error handling assumes partial failure is normal in distributed systems.
  • Configuration externalizes environment-specific values.
Part 10

Spring & Cloud Integration

Spring Boot and Spring Cloud express Software Architecture Basics with production defaults:

@SpringBootApplication
public class FulfillmentApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(FulfillmentApplication.class, args);
    }
}

@Configuration
class ArchitectureBeans {
    @Bean OrderCapability orders(OrderRepository repo, PaymentPort port) {
        return new OrderCapability(repo, port);
    }
}

Spring Stack Mapping

Concern Spring Module
HTTP APIs Spring Web / WebFlux
Resilience Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker, Resilience4j
Discovery Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, Eureka/Consul
Config Spring Cloud Config, Kubernetes ConfigMaps
Part 11

Cloud Deployment

On AWS, architecture maps to accounts/VPCs per environment, EKS namespaces per domain, and IAM boundaries. Landing zones enforce guardrails so teams cannot bypass network isolation.

Kubernetes Notes

Resource Role
Deployment Rolling updates per service
Service Stable cluster DNS for pods
Ingress / Gateway Edge routing, TLS, rate limits
HPA Autoscale on CPU, memory, or custom metrics
Part 12

Production Usage

JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs run architecture review boards for cross-cutting changes; Netflix's Architecture Team publishes standards for resilient, observable services before teams adopt new patterns org-wide.

Production Checklist

  • [ ] Define SLOs and error budgets before scaling teams
  • [ ] Document data ownership and consistency guarantees
  • [ ] Run game days for dependency failure scenarios
  • [ ] Automate rollbacks and health-gated deploys
Part 13

Architect Perspective

Lead with quality attributes and failure domains, not technology labels. The architect's job is to preserve option value: allow evolution without rewrite.

ADR Prompts

  1. What problem does Software Architecture Basics solve that simpler structure cannot?
  2. What is the rollback plan if the pattern increases operational load?
  3. Which metric proves the pattern is working six months later?
Part 14

Decision Matrix

Choosing Software Architecture Basics versus alternatives:

Option Strength Trade-off
Monolith first Fast iteration, strong consistency Becomes release bottleneck
Microservices early Team autonomy Operational tax before product-market fit
Modular monolith Clear modules, single deploy Requires discipline to avoid coupling

When to Choose Software Architecture Basics

Use when team boundaries, release independence, or failure isolation justify the integration tax. Defer when the domain is small, the team is unified, and transactional consistency dominates.

Part 15

Comparison Tables

Side-by-side view for Software Architecture Basics:

Monolith first: Fast iteration, strong consistency — trade-off: Becomes release bottleneck. Microservices early: Team autonomy — trade-off: Operational tax before product-market fit. Modular monolith: Clear modules, single deploy — trade-off: Requires discipline to avoid coupling.

Lens Software Architecture Basics Typical Alternative
Deploy unit Service or module boundary Single deployable
Data Owned schema per boundary Shared database
Consistency Eventual + sagas common Local ACID
Ops complexity Higher — more moving parts Lower until scale hits
Part 16

Common Mistakes

Teams stumble on Software Architecture Basics when:

  • Choosing microservices to skip domain modeling
  • Architecture driven by vendor slides instead of constraints
  • No measurable quality attributes in ADRs
Mistake Fix
Boundary by technology Boundary by business capability
Shared mutable database Database per service or strict schema ownership
Sync chains without timeouts Deadline propagation and bulkheads

Part 1

Concept

Monolith — A monolith is a single deployable application containing most or all business capabilities in one runtime process.

Monoliths are not inherently bad — they are the default successful shape for new products. Shopify's core commerce platform remained a modular monolith for years while serving massive GMV because a unified deployable minimized distributed consistency problems.

Mental Model

+--------------------------- MONOLITH ---------------------------+
|  Controllers / API                                           |
|  +----------+  +----------+  +----------+  +----------+      |
|  | Orders   |  | Catalog  |  | Payments |  | Users    |      |
|  +----+-----+  +----+-----+  +----+-----+  +----+-----+      |
|       \            |              |            /             |
|        v           v              v           v              |
|              +---------------------------+                   |
|              |     Shared Database       |                   |
|              +---------------------------+                   |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

Key Terms

Term Definition
Single deployable One artifact (WAR/JAR/container) released to production.
Shared database One schema accessed by multiple modules — common in monoliths.
Modular monolith Monolith with enforced module boundaries and explicit APIs.
Release train Coordinated cadence shipping the entire application together.
Blast radius Scope of impact when a defect or deployment fails.

Why Architects Care

  • Monolith shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How Monolith evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
1990s Java EE WAR/EAR on WebLogic All tiers packaged together
2005 Rails/Django monoliths Rapid CRUD products in one repo
2014 Microservices hype Monolith labeled as anti-pattern
2018 Modular monolith revival DHH, Shopify, Thoughtworks advocate structured monoliths
2024 AI-assisted refactors Strangler extraction from proven monolith modules

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt Monolith because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do we ship features quickly when every change risks redeploying the entire application?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. Unbounded shared mutable state between modules
  2. Schema changes blocking unrelated teams
  3. Long startup times as codebase grows
  4. Single thread pool exhaustion affecting all features
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

Monoliths exist because local method calls, single-database transactions, and unified debugging are dramatically simpler than distributed systems. They are the rational default until team or scale constraints make the coupling cost higher than the distribution tax.

Design Goals

Goal How Monolith Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for Monolith follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

+--------------------------- MONOLITH ---------------------------+
|  Controllers / API                                           |
|  +----------+  +----------+  +----------+  +----------+      |
|  | Orders   |  | Catalog  |  | Payments |  | Users    |      |
|  +----+-----+  +----+-----+  +----+-----+  +----+-----+      |
|       \            |              |            /             |
|        v           v              v           v              |
|              +---------------------------+                   |
|              |     Shared Database       |                   |
|              +---------------------------+                   |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

Step-by-Step

  1. HTTP/API layer routes to application services
  2. Domain logic executes in-process
  3. Persistence uses shared ORM/session
  4. Background jobs run in same JVM or sidecar worker
  5. Single CI pipeline produces one artifact

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges
Part 6

Failure Modes

When Monolith is misapplied, these failures appear repeatedly:

  • Unbounded shared mutable state between modules
  • Schema changes blocking unrelated teams
  • Long startup times as codebase grows
  • Single thread pool exhaustion affecting all features

Incident Pattern

User request ──► missing timeout ──► thread pool exhaustion ──► cascading 503s
                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges
Part 7

Scale Considerations

Monolith at Amazon/Netflix/Uber scale requires explicit capacity thinking:

  • Vertical scaling + read replicas extend monolith life
  • Shopify shards by shop_id while keeping logical monolith
  • Feature flags decouple deploy from release inside monolith

Scale Checklist

Dimension Question to Answer
Throughput What RPS per instance before saturation?
Data growth Which store becomes the bottleneck first?
Fan-out How many downstream calls per request?
Multi-region What consistency trade-off is acceptable?
Part 8

Performance

Performance for Monolith is dominated by integration cost, not local CPU:

  • In-process calls avoid serialization overhead
  • Connection pool contention hits all modules
  • GC pauses affect entire JVM — profile holistically
Factor Typical Impact Mitigation
Network hops +1–5 ms per sync call Cache, batch, async where safe
Serialization CPU on large payloads Schema evolution, compression
Connection pools Queueing under burst Pool sizing + backpressure
Part 9

Java Example

Representative Java illustrating Monolith:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
class OrderController {
    private final OrderService service;
    OrderController(OrderService service) { this.service = service; }

    @PostMapping
    ResponseEntity<OrderView> create(@RequestBody CreateOrderRequest req) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(service.create(req));
    }
}

Reading the Example

  • Notice explicit boundaries — domain code does not reach into foreign persistence.
  • Error handling assumes partial failure is normal in distributed systems.
  • Configuration externalizes environment-specific values.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Pattern Exists5Internal Working6Failure Modes7Scale Considerations8Performance9Java Example10Spring & Cloud Integration11Cloud Deployment12Production Usage13Architect Perspective14Decision Matrix15Comparison Tables16Common Mistakes17Interview Questions18Revision Sheet19Execution Flow20Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Layered Architecture — Layered architecture organizes code into horizontal tiers — typically presentation, application, domain, and infrastructure.

The classic four-layer model (UI → application → domain → infrastructure) enforces dependency direction: inner layers never depend on outer layers. Spring MVC apps often mirror this with controllers, services, repositories, and entities — but violations (domain calling JDBC) collapse the model.

Mental Model

+--------------------------------------------------+
| Presentation  (Controllers, GraphQL resolvers)   |
+--------------------------------------------------+
| Application   (Use cases, @Transactional)      |
+--------------------------------------------------+
| Domain        (Entities, value objects, rules)   |
+--------------------------------------------------+
| Infrastructure (JPA, Kafka, REST clients)        |
+--------------------------------------------------+
         dependencies point DOWN only -->

Key Terms

Term Definition
Presentation layer HTTP, gRPC handlers, DTO mapping.
Application layer Use cases, orchestration, transaction boundaries.
Domain layer Business rules, entities, domain services.
Infrastructure layer DB, messaging, external APIs — implements ports.
Dependency rule Inner layers never import outer layers.

Why Architects Care

  • Layered Architecture shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How Layered Architecture evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
1970s OSI-inspired layering Separation of concerns in telecom/software
1990s 3-tier enterprise Client, app server, database
2003 DDD layered model Evans formalizes domain-centric layers
2010s Hexagonal/clean variants Ports and adapters rename layers
2020s Package-by-feature pushback Layers vs vertical slices debate

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt Layered Architecture because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do we prevent UI and database concerns from leaking into core business rules?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. Anemic domain model — all logic in services
  2. Layer bypass — controller calls repository directly
  3. God service class spanning every use case
  4. DTO explosion without clear mapping boundaries
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

Without layers, SQL strings appear in controllers and business logic becomes untestable. Layers create test seams: swap infrastructure with fakes while keeping domain pure.

Design Goals

Goal How Layered Architecture Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for Layered Architecture follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

+--------------------------------------------------+
| Presentation  (Controllers, GraphQL resolvers)   |
+--------------------------------------------------+
| Application   (Use cases, @Transactional)      |
+--------------------------------------------------+
| Domain        (Entities, value objects, rules)   |
+--------------------------------------------------+
| Infrastructure (JPA, Kafka, REST clients)        |
+--------------------------------------------------+
         dependencies point DOWN only -->

Step-by-Step

  1. Request enters presentation layer
  2. Application service loads aggregates via repositories
  3. Domain enforces invariants and emits domain events
  4. Infrastructure persists changes and publishes messages
  5. Response mapped to DTO at edge

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges
Part 6

Failure Modes

When Layered Architecture is misapplied, these failures appear repeatedly:

  • Anemic domain model — all logic in services
  • Layer bypass — controller calls repository directly
  • God service class spanning every use case
  • DTO explosion without clear mapping boundaries

Incident Pattern

User request ──► missing timeout ──► thread pool exhaustion ──► cascading 503s
                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges
Part 7

Scale Considerations

Layered Architecture at Amazon/Netflix/Uber scale requires explicit capacity thinking:

  • Layers don't scale horizontally — deployables do
  • Separate read models may bypass strict layers for queries
  • Caching often sits at presentation or infrastructure edge

Scale Checklist

Dimension Question to Answer
Throughput What RPS per instance before saturation?
Data growth Which store becomes the bottleneck first?
Fan-out How many downstream calls per request?
Multi-region What consistency trade-off is acceptable?
Part 8

Performance

Performance for Layered Architecture is dominated by integration cost, not local CPU:

  • Extra mapping between layers adds CPU
  • Transaction boundaries at application layer affect lock duration
  • N+1 queries originate in infrastructure misconfiguration
Factor Typical Impact Mitigation
Network hops +1–5 ms per sync call Cache, batch, async where safe
Serialization CPU on large payloads Schema evolution, compression
Connection pools Queueing under burst Pool sizing + backpressure
Part 9

Java Example

Representative Java illustrating Layered Architecture:

public final class Money { private final BigDecimal amount; public Money add(Money o) { return this; } }

Reading the Example

  • Notice explicit boundaries — domain code does not reach into foreign persistence.
  • Error handling assumes partial failure is normal in distributed systems.
  • Configuration externalizes environment-specific values.
Part 10

Spring & Cloud Integration

Spring Boot and Spring Cloud express Layered Architecture with production defaults:

@RestController class TransferController { private final TransferFunds useCase; @PostMapping("/transfers") void transfer(@RequestBody TransferRequest dto) { useCase.execute(dto); } }

Spring Stack Mapping

Concern Spring Module
HTTP APIs Spring Web / WebFlux
Resilience Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker, Resilience4j
Discovery Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, Eureka/Consul
Config Spring Cloud Config, Kubernetes ConfigMaps
Part 11

Cloud Deployment

Layered monolith in one container is fine; observability tags spans by layer (controller vs repo).

Kubernetes Notes

Resource Role
Deployment Rolling updates per service
Service Stable cluster DNS for pods
Ingress / Gateway Edge routing, TLS, rate limits
HPA Autoscale on CPU, memory, or custom metrics
Part 12

Production Usage

Many bank cores use strict layering for auditability — domain changes require compliance review.

Production Checklist

  • [ ] Define SLOs and error budgets before scaling teams
  • [ ] Document data ownership and consistency guarantees
  • [ ] Run game days for dependency failure scenarios
  • [ ] Automate rollbacks and health-gated deploys
Part 13

Architect Perspective

Layers are a dependency rule, not a folder religion. Enforce with ArchUnit or module boundaries.

ADR Prompts

  1. What problem does Layered Architecture solve that simpler structure cannot?
  2. What is the rollback plan if the pattern increases operational load?
  3. Which metric proves the pattern is working six months later?
Part 14

Decision Matrix

Choosing Layered Architecture versus alternatives:

Option Strength Trade-off
Hexagonal Ports face outward Steeper learning curve
Vertical slice Feature colocation Risk of cross-slice duplication
Clean architecture Entities at center Ceremony for small apps

When to Choose Layered Architecture

Use when team boundaries, release independence, or failure isolation justify the integration tax. Defer when the domain is small, the team is unified, and transactional consistency dominates.

Part 15

Comparison Tables

Side-by-side view for Layered Architecture:

Hexagonal: Ports face outward — trade-off: Steeper learning curve. Vertical slice: Feature colocation — trade-off: Risk of cross-slice duplication. Clean architecture: Entities at center — trade-off: Ceremony for small apps.

Lens Layered Architecture Typical Alternative
Deploy unit Service or module boundary Single deployable
Data Owned schema per boundary Shared database
Consistency Eventual + sagas common Local ACID
Ops complexity Higher — more moving parts Lower until scale hits
Part 16

Common Mistakes

Teams stumble on Layered Architecture when:

  • Creating layer for every possible abstraction
  • Transactional annotations on controllers
  • Domain importing Spring Data interfaces
Mistake Fix
Boundary by technology Boundary by business capability
Shared mutable database Database per service or strict schema ownership
Sync chains without timeouts Deadline propagation and bulkheads

Architect Level

  2. Audit trail across layers.
Part 18

Revision Sheet

Eight bullets to remember Layered Architecture:

  • Dependencies flow inward/downward only
  • Domain holds business rules — keep framework out
  • Application orchestrates use cases and transactions
  • Infrastructure implements ports — swappable
  • Layers are not deployables — don't confuse with services
  • ArchUnit enforces what conventions cannot
  • Anemic domain is a smell — push logic down
  • Vertical slices can coexist with layer rules per slice

One-Minute Drill

  2. Name two failure modes from Part 6.

Execution Flow

End-to-end flow for Layered Architecture:

Client ──► Edge ──► Service ──► Owned Store
              │         │
              │         └── Request enters presentation layer → Application service loads aggregates via repositories → Domain enforces invariants and emits domain events → Infrastructure persists changes and publishes messages
              └── auth, rate limit, routing

Trace one request through logging and metrics — each hop should have a span and a timeout budget.

Part 1

Concept

SOA — Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) organizes capabilities as loosely coupled, discoverable services with explicit contracts, often orchestrated through an Enterprise Service Bus.

SOA emerged when enterprises needed to integrate ERP, CRM, and legacy mainframes without rewriting everything. Services expose WSDL/SOAP or REST contracts; an ESB routes, transforms, and mediates messages. Amazon's early internal SOA (2002) mandated that teams expose data only via service interfaces — a direct precursor to microservices.

Mental Model

[CRM] -->\                    /--> [Billing Svc]
[ERP] --> --> [ ESB / API ] --> --> [ Inventory Svc]
[Web] -->/                    \--> [ Legacy Adapter ]

Key Terms

Term Definition
Service contract WSDL/OpenAPI defining operations and schemas.
ESB Enterprise Service Bus — central message router and adapter.
Loose coupling Services interact via interfaces, not shared code.
Service registry UDDI or modern equivalent for discovery.
Orchestration Coordinating multiple services into a business process.

Why Architects Care

  • SOA shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How SOA evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
2000s SOAP + WSDL + UDDI Vendor-neutral web services stack
2005 ESB peak (Mule, Tibco) Central hub for transformation
2010 REST overtakes SOAP JSON APIs simplify integration
2015 Microservices backlash to SOA ESB seen as bottleneck
2020 Event-driven SOA hybrid Kafka replaces heavy ESB for async

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt SOA because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do heterogeneous systems (COBOL, Java, SAP) participate in one business process without point-to-point spaghetti?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. ESB becomes single point of failure and bottleneck
  2. Canonical data model debates stall projects for years
  3. Shared ESB team becomes integration gatekeeper
  4. Versioning all services in lockstep via ESB config
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

Point-to-point integration creates N² connections; SOA introduces a contract-first layer so consumers depend on interfaces, not implementations. ESB handles protocol and schema translation centrally.

Design Goals

Goal How SOA Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for SOA follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

[CRM] -->\                    /--> [Billing Svc]
[ERP] --> --> [ ESB / API ] --> --> [ Inventory Svc]
[Web] -->/                    \--> [ Legacy Adapter ]

Step-by-Step

  1. Consumer resolves service from registry
  2. Request sent to ESB or direct to service endpoint
  3. ESB transforms message format if needed
  4. Service executes business logic and returns response
  5. ESB routes response back to consumer

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges
Part 6

Failure Modes

When SOA is misapplied, these failures appear repeatedly:

  • ESB becomes single point of failure and bottleneck
  • Canonical data model debates stall projects for years
  • Shared ESB team becomes integration gatekeeper
  • Versioning all services in lockstep via ESB config

Incident Pattern

User request ──► missing timeout ──► thread pool exhaustion ──► cascading 503s
                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges
Part 7

Scale Considerations

SOA at Amazon/Netflix/Uber scale requires explicit capacity thinking:

  • FedEx integrated shipping across acquisitions via SOA
  • Large banks still run ESB for SWIFT/payment rails
  • Decompose ESB into API gateway + event bus at scale

Scale Checklist

Dimension Question to Answer
Throughput What RPS per instance before saturation?
Data growth Which store becomes the bottleneck first?
Fan-out How many downstream calls per request?
Multi-region What consistency trade-off is acceptable?
Part 8

Performance

Performance for SOA is dominated by integration cost, not local CPU:

  • ESB XML transformation adds 10-50ms per hop
  • Synchronous SOA chains amplify tail latency
  • Cache service responses at consumer edge
Factor Typical Impact Mitigation
Network hops +1–5 ms per sync call Cache, batch, async where safe
Serialization CPU on large payloads Schema evolution, compression
Connection pools Queueing under burst Pool sizing + backpressure
Part 9

Java Example

Representative Java illustrating SOA:

@WebService public class PaymentService { @WebMethod public PaymentResult charge(ChargeRequest req) { return gateway.charge(req); } }

Reading the Example

  • Notice explicit boundaries — domain code does not reach into foreign persistence.
  • Error handling assumes partial failure is normal in distributed systems.
  • Configuration externalizes environment-specific values.

Wells Fargo and HSBC used SOA to wrap core banking while exposing mobile channels; Amazon's 2002 API mandate forced service boundaries before microservices had a name.

Production Checklist

  • [ ] Define SLOs and error budgets before scaling teams
  • [ ] Document data ownership and consistency guarantees
  • [ ] Run game days for dependency failure scenarios
  • [ ] Automate rollbacks and health-gated deploys
Part 13

Architect Perspective

Use SOA thinking for contract-first integration; avoid rebuilding a monolithic ESB — prefer smart endpoints and dumb pipes (Kafka).

ADR Prompts

  1. What problem does SOA solve that simpler structure cannot?
  2. What is the rollback plan if the pattern increases operational load?
  3. Which metric proves the pattern is working six months later?

Option Strength Trade-off
Point-to-point REST Simple, no hub N² integration pain
Microservices Fine-grained autonomy Higher ops overhead
iPaaS (MuleSoft) Managed integration Vendor cost and lock-in

When to Choose SOA

Use when team boundaries, release independence, or failure isolation justify the integration tax. Defer when the domain is small, the team is unified, and transactional consistency dominates.

Point-to-point REST: Simple, no hub — trade-off: N² integration pain. Microservices: Fine-grained autonomy — trade-off: Higher ops overhead. iPaaS (MuleSoft): Managed integration — trade-off: Vendor cost and lock-in.

Lens SOA Typical Alternative
Deploy unit Service or module boundary Single deployable
Data Owned schema per boundary Shared database
Consistency Eventual + sagas common Local ACID
Ops complexity Higher — more moving parts Lower until scale hits

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Pattern Exists5Internal Working6Failure Modes7Scale Considerations8Performance9Java Example10Spring & Cloud Integration11Cloud Deployment12Production Usage13Architect Perspective14Decision Matrix15Comparison Tables16Common Mistakes17Interview Questions18Revision Sheet19Execution Flow20Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Microservices — Microservices is an architectural style structuring an application as a collection of small, independently deployable services aligned to business capabilities.

Each microservice owns its data, runs in its own process, and communicates over lightweight protocols (HTTP, gRPC, messaging). Netflix pioneered operational patterns (Chaos Monkey, Zuul) that made microservices viable at scale. The style trades distributed complexity for team autonomy and independent release cadence.

Mental Model

+----------+
  Client ---------> | Gateway  |
                    +----+-----+
         +-------------+-------------+
         v             v             v
    [Orders]      [Payments]     [Inventory]
         |             |             |
    [Order DB]    [Pay DB]      [Inv DB]

Key Terms

Term Definition
Bounded capability Service maps to one business function (payments, catalog).
Independent deploy Release one service without redeploying others.
Decentralized data Each service owns its database schema.
Smart endpoints Services expose APIs; network is dumb pipe.
Design for failure Assume partial outages; use resilience patterns.

Why Architects Care

  • Microservices shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How Microservices evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
2011 Netflix OSS stack Eureka, Hystrix, Zuul popularize patterns
2014 Martin Fowler microservices article Industry vocabulary crystallizes
2016 Kubernetes GA Container orchestration lowers ops bar
2019 DHH 'Microservices regret' Backlash at small scale
2023 Platform engineering Golden paths standardize microservice scaffolding

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt Microservices because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do dozens of teams ship daily without stepping on each other's releases or corrupting shared state?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. Distributed monolith — services deployed separately but tightly coupled
  2. No data ownership — multiple services write same tables
  3. Chatty synchronous chains causing latency cascades
  4. Operational overhead exceeds team capacity
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

Monolith release trains and shared databases become coordination bottlenecks at org scale. Microservices decouple deployables and data ownership so teams optimize locally while integrating via stable contracts.

Design Goals

Goal How Microservices Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for Microservices follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

+----------+
  Client ---------> | Gateway  |
                    +----+-----+
         +-------------+-------------+
         v             v             v
    [Orders]      [Payments]     [Inventory]
         |             |             |
    [Order DB]    [Pay DB]      [Inv DB]

Step-by-Step

  1. Client hits API gateway or BFF
  2. Gateway routes to target service instance via discovery
  3. Service executes logic against its private database
  4. Cross-service calls use sync HTTP or async events
  5. Observability correlates trace across hop boundaries

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges
Part 6

Failure Modes

When Microservices is misapplied, these failures appear repeatedly:

  • Distributed monolith — services deployed separately but tightly coupled
  • No data ownership — multiple services write same tables
  • Chatty synchronous chains causing latency cascades
  • Operational overhead exceeds team capacity

Incident Pattern

User request ──► missing timeout ──► thread pool exhaustion ──► cascading 503s
                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges
Part 7

Scale Considerations

Microservices at Amazon/Netflix/Uber scale requires explicit capacity thinking:

  • Netflix runs 700+ microservices with dedicated tooling teams
  • Uber domain-aligned services map to 2000+ deployables
  • Service mesh handles cross-cutting concerns at scale

Scale Checklist

Dimension Question to Answer
Throughput What RPS per instance before saturation?
Data growth Which store becomes the bottleneck first?
Fan-out How many downstream calls per request?
Multi-region What consistency trade-off is acceptable?
Part 8

Performance

Performance for Microservices is dominated by integration cost, not local CPU:

  • Each hop adds network RTT and serialization cost
  • Fan-out queries need scatter-gather or GraphQL BFF
  • Connection pool sizing per service affects cluster memory
Factor Typical Impact Mitigation
Network hops +1–5 ms per sync call Cache, batch, async where safe
Serialization CPU on large payloads Schema evolution, compression
Connection pools Queueing under burst Pool sizing + backpressure

Reading the Example

  • Notice explicit boundaries — domain code does not reach into foreign persistence.
  • Error handling assumes partial failure is normal in distributed systems.
  • Configuration externalizes environment-specific values.

Part 1

Concept

12-Factor Applications — The Twelve-Factor App methodology defines twelve practices for building cloud-native, portable, scalable applications as stateless processes.

Heroku engineers codified these principles in 2011: one codebase, explicit dependencies, environment config, backing services as attached resources, build/release/run separation, stateless processes, port binding, concurrency via process model, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs as streams, and admin tasks as one-off processes.

Mental Model

[Git Repo] --> [CI Build] --> [Artifact]
                                  |
                    Config (env vars / secrets)
                                  v
                         [Release] --> [Process 1]
                                     --> [Process 2]
                                     --> [Process N]

Key Terms

Term Definition
Factor III Config Store config in environment, not code.
Factor VI Processes Execute app as one or more stateless processes.
Factor IX Disposability Fast startup and graceful shutdown.
Factor IV Backing services Treat DB/cache/queue as attached resources.
Factor X Dev/prod parity Keep development and production as similar as possible.

Why Architects Care

  • 12-Factor Applications shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How 12-Factor Applications evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
2007 Heroku platform launch Opinionated Ruby deploy model
2011 12-Factor manifesto published Cloud-native vocabulary
2014 Docker adoption Factor V build/release/run in containers
2018 Kubernetes ConfigMaps/Secrets Factor III in orchestrators
2022 Platform engineering 12-factor embedded in golden paths

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt 12-Factor Applications because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do we build apps that deploy consistently across environments without config drift and secret leaks?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. Config in source control leaking secrets
  2. Sticky sessions breaking horizontal scale
  3. Slow startup preventing fast autoscaling
  4. Local filesystem used as durable state store
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

Traditional apps embed config in code or WAR files, bind to local paths, and assume long-lived servers. Cloud platforms need portable artifacts where environment differences are injected at runtime, not baked into builds.

Design Goals

Goal How 12-Factor Applications Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for 12-Factor Applications follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

[Git Repo] --> [CI Build] --> [Artifact]
                                  |
                    Config (env vars / secrets)
                                  v
                         [Release] --> [Process 1]
                                     --> [Process 2]
                                     --> [Process N]

Step-by-Step

  1. Code pushed to VCS triggers CI build
  2. Build produces immutable artifact with pinned dependencies
  3. Release stage combines artifact + config
  4. Runtime processes start stateless workers bound to PORT
  5. Logs stream to aggregator; admin tasks run as one-off jobs

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges

  • Local filesystem used as durable state store

                      │

Part 1

Concept

Domain Driven Design — Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is a software design approach centering development on a rich model of the business domain, using ubiquitous language shared by developers and domain experts.

Eric Evans' 2003 book introduced entities, value objects, aggregates, repositories, and domain events. DDD separates generic subdomains (auth, billing infra) from core domain differentiators. Strategic DDD (contexts, boundaries) pairs with tactical patterns (aggregates, factories) to keep complexity manageable.

Mental Model

+------------------------------------------------+
|           Ubiquitous Language                  |
|  Order | LineItem | Money | Fulfillment        |
+------------------------------------------------+
|  Aggregate: Order (root) + LineItems           |
|  Invariants: total = sum(lines), min order $10 |
+------------------------------------------------+
|  Repository port  |  Domain events out         |
+------------------------------------------------+

Key Terms

Term Definition
Ubiquitous language Shared vocabulary between devs and business.
Aggregate Cluster of entities with consistency boundary.
Bounded context Explicit boundary where a model applies.
Entity Object with identity persisting over time.
Value object Immutable object defined by attributes.

Why Architects Care

  • Domain Driven Design shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How Domain Driven Design evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
2003 Evans publishes DDD book Tactical + strategic patterns
2008 CQRS emerges Separate read/write models in complex domains
2013 Event sourcing adoption Domain events as source of truth
2017 DDD in microservices Context maps guide service splits
2022 DDD + data mesh Domain ownership extends to analytics

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt Domain Driven Design because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do we prevent software models from diverging from how the business actually thinks and operates?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. Anemic domain — entities are getters/setters only
  2. Aggregate too large — entire system in one root
  3. Context bleed — one model forced across departments
  4. Event storming without follow-through to code
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

CRUD-driven designs mirror database tables, not business rules. DDD embeds domain expertise in code through explicit models, invariants, and language — reducing miscommunication that causes expensive rework.

Design Goals

Goal How Domain Driven Design Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for Domain Driven Design follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

+------------------------------------------------+
|           Ubiquitous Language                  |
|  Order | LineItem | Money | Fulfillment        |
+------------------------------------------------+
|  Aggregate: Order (root) + LineItems           |
|  Invariants: total = sum(lines), min order $10 |
+------------------------------------------------+
|  Repository port  |  Domain events out         |
+------------------------------------------------+

Step-by-Step

  1. Event storming or interviews capture domain language
  2. Identify aggregates and consistency boundaries
  3. Model entities and value objects with invariants
  4. Define repositories and domain services
  5. Publish domain events for cross-context integration

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges

When Domain Driven Design is misapplied, these failures appear repeatedly:

  • Anemic domain — entities are getters/setters only
  • Aggregate too large — entire system in one root
  • Context bleed — one model forced across departments
  • Event storming without follow-through to code

Incident Pattern

User request ──► missing timeout ──► thread pool exhaustion ──► cascading 503s
                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges

  • Domain logic in entities avoids service layer bloat
  • Event-driven integration avoids synchronous coupling
Factor Typical Impact Mitigation

Serialization CPU on large payloads Schema evolution, compression
Connection pools Queueing under burst Pool sizing + backpressure

Part 1

Concept

Bounded Context — A bounded context is an explicit boundary within which a particular domain model is defined and applicable, with its own ubiquitous language and integration contracts at the edges.

The same word (Customer, Product) means different things in Sales vs Shipping vs Billing. Bounded contexts make these differences explicit. Context maps document relationships: shared kernel, customer-supplier, anti-corruption layer, open-host service.

Mental Model

+-------------+     ACL      +-------------+
|   Sales     | <---------> |  Fulfillment |
|  "Customer" |             |  "Recipient" |
+-------------+             +-------------+
       |                           |
       +-------- Context Map -------+

Key Terms

Term Definition
Context map Diagram of context relationships and integration patterns.
Anti-corruption layer Translation layer protecting model from external schemas.
Shared kernel Small shared model between two contexts.
Open host service Published integration API for multiple consumers.
Partnership Two contexts evolving together with mutual dependency.

Why Architects Care

  • Bounded Context shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How Bounded Context evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
2003 Evans introduces bounded context Strategic DDD foundation
2010 Context mapping workshops Event storming popularizes boundaries
2015 Microservices = contexts hype One service per context ideal
2019 Domain-driven microservices ACL at every integration point
2023 Federated governance Context ownership in data mesh

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt Bounded Context because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do we integrate teams and systems when the same term means different things in different departments?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. One global canonical model forced on all teams
  2. ACL skipped — external schema leaks into domain
  3. Context boundaries match org chart but not domain
  4. Microservice per entity instead of per context
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

Without bounded contexts, teams force one canonical model that fits nobody. Contexts allow optimized local models with explicit translation at boundaries — reducing both coupling and semantic confusion.

Design Goals

Goal How Bounded Context Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for Bounded Context follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

+-------------+     ACL      +-------------+
|   Sales     | <---------> |  Fulfillment |
|  "Customer" |             |  "Recipient" |
+-------------+             +-------------+
       |                           |
       +-------- Context Map -------+

Step-by-Step

  1. Identify subdomains and assign bounded contexts
  2. Define ubiquitous language per context
  3. Draw context map with integration relationships
  4. Implement ACL or published language at boundaries
  5. Evolve contexts independently with contract tests

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges
Part 6

Failure Modes

When Bounded Context is misapplied, these failures appear repeatedly:

  • One global canonical model forced on all teams
  • ACL skipped — external schema leaks into domain
  • Context boundaries match org chart but not domain
  • Microservice per entity instead of per context

Incident Pattern

User request ──► missing timeout ──► thread pool exhaustion ──► cascading 503s
                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges
Part 7

Scale Considerations

Bounded Context at Amazon/Netflix/Uber scale requires explicit capacity thinking:

  • Amazon service boundaries follow business capabilities
  • Spotify squad contexts map to bounded domains
  • SAP vs custom apps connected via ACL in enterprises

Scale Checklist

Dimension Question to Answer
Throughput What RPS per instance before saturation?
Data growth Which store becomes the bottleneck first?
Fan-out How many downstream calls per request?
Multi-region What consistency trade-off is acceptable?
Part 8

Performance

Performance for Bounded Context is dominated by integration cost, not local CPU:

  • ACL adds mapping overhead but prevents model corruption
  • Separate contexts enable independent schema evolution
  • Published language reduces N custom integrations
Factor Typical Impact Mitigation
Network hops +1–5 ms per sync call Cache, batch, async where safe
Serialization CPU on large payloads Schema evolution, compression
Connection pools Queueing under burst Pool sizing + backpressure
Part 9

Java Example

Representative Java illustrating Bounded Context:

public class SalesCustomer { /* marketing attributes */ } public class FulfillmentRecipient { /* shipping address */ } public class CustomerAcl { FulfillmentRecipient toRecipient(SalesCustomer c) { ... } }

Reading the Example

  • Notice explicit boundaries — domain code does not reach into foreign persistence.
  • Error handling assumes partial failure is normal in distributed systems.
  • Configuration externalizes environment-specific values.

Spring Boot and Spring Cloud express Bounded Context with production defaults:

Resource Role

Part 14

Decision Matrix

Choosing Bounded Context versus alternatives:

Option Strength Trade-off
Single unified model One source of truth illusion Lowest common denominator design
Integration database Easy queries Coupling nightmare
Shared library models DRY Hidden coupling across contexts

When to Choose Bounded Context

Use when team boundaries, release independence, or failure isolation justify the integration tax. Defer when the domain is small, the team is unified, and transactional consistency dominates.

Part 15

Comparison Tables

Side-by-side view for Bounded Context:

Single unified model: One source of truth illusion — trade-off: Lowest common denominator design. Integration database: Easy queries — trade-off: Coupling nightmare. Shared library models: DRY — trade-off: Hidden coupling across contexts.

Lens Bounded Context Typical Alternative
Deploy unit Service or module boundary Single deployable
Data Owned schema per boundary Shared database
Consistency Eventual + sagas common Local ACID
Ops complexity Higher — more moving parts Lower until scale hits
Part 16

Common Mistakes

Teams stumble on Bounded Context when:

  • Confusing bounded context with microservice (1:1 not required)
  • No ACL when integrating legacy ERP
  • Context map never updated after org restructure
Mistake Fix
Boundary by technology Boundary by business capability
Shared mutable database Database per service or strict schema ownership
Sync chains without timeouts Deadline propagation and bulkheads

Part 1

Concept

Database per Service — Database per Service assigns each microservice exclusive ownership of its data store — no other service reads or writes that database directly.

This pattern enforces encapsulation at the persistence layer. Other services access data only through the owning service's API or events. Amazon popularized 'each service owns its data' as a hard rule — violating it creates hidden coupling that defeats independent deployability.

Mental Model

[Order Svc] --> [Order DB]
[Payment Svc] --> [Payment DB]
[Inventory Svc] --> [Inventory DB]

Order Svc --HTTP--> Payment Svc (never Payment DB)
Order Svc <--event-- Inventory Svc

Key Terms

Term Definition
Data ownership Only one service mutates a given dataset.
Private schema Database not accessible to other services' credentials.
Integration via API Cross-service reads go through HTTP/gRPC.
Event replication Downstream caches updated from domain events.
Schema evolution Owner migrates schema without coordinating all consumers.

Why Architects Care

  • Database per Service shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How Database per Service evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
2012 Microservices early adopters Shared DB anti-pattern identified
2015 Martin Fowler database per service Pattern catalog entry
2018 Saga + event sourcing Cross-service consistency without shared TX
2020 Data mesh Domain-oriented decentralized data
2023 Database branching Neon/PlanetScale per-service workflows

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt Database per Service because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do services evolve schemas and deploy independently when they all touch the same database?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. Distributed joins attempted via direct DB access
  2. Reporting needs force shared read replicas violating ownership
  3. Saga failures leave inconsistent cross-service state
  4. Duplicate data without event-driven sync strategy
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

Shared databases let services bypass APIs and create implicit contracts via SQL joins. Database per service makes integration explicit — through APIs and events — enabling true independent evolution.

Design Goals

Goal How Database per Service Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for Database per Service follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

[Order Svc] --> [Order DB]
[Payment Svc] --> [Payment DB]
[Inventory Svc] --> [Inventory DB]

Order Svc --HTTP--> Payment Svc (never Payment DB)
Order Svc <--event-- Inventory Svc

Step-by-Step

  1. Service receives request for its domain data
  2. Query/update only local private database
  3. Cross-domain needs call peer service API
  4. Domain events publish state changes to subscribers
  5. Consumers maintain local read models from events

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges
Part 6

Failure Modes

When Database per Service is misapplied, these failures appear repeatedly:

  • Distributed joins attempted via direct DB access
  • Reporting needs force shared read replicas violating ownership
  • Saga failures leave inconsistent cross-service state
  • Duplicate data without event-driven sync strategy

Incident Pattern

User request ──► missing timeout ──► thread pool exhaustion ──► cascading 503s
                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges
Part 7

Scale Considerations

Database per Service at Amazon/Netflix/Uber scale requires explicit capacity thinking:

  • Netflix: no cross-service database access policy
  • Uber each domain owns Cassandra/MySQL clusters
  • Read models via CDC from service databases

Scale Checklist

Dimension Question to Answer
Throughput What RPS per instance before saturation?
Data growth Which store becomes the bottleneck first?
Fan-out How many downstream calls per request?
Multi-region What consistency trade-off is acceptable?
Part 8

Performance

Performance for Database per Service is dominated by integration cost, not local CPU:

  • No cross-DB joins — accept denormalized read models
  • Connection pools sized per service not global
  • Eventual consistency reads may lag primary writes
Factor Typical Impact Mitigation
Network hops +1–5 ms per sync call Cache, batch, async where safe
Serialization CPU on large payloads Schema evolution, compression
Connection pools Queueing under burst Pool sizing + backpressure

Reading the Example

  • Notice explicit boundaries — domain code does not reach into foreign persistence.
  • Error handling assumes partial failure is normal in distributed systems.
  • Configuration externalizes environment-specific values.

When to Choose Database per Service

Use when team boundaries, release independence, or failure isolation justify the integration tax. Defer when the domain is small, the team is unified, and transactional consistency dominates.

Shared database: Easy cross-domain queries — trade-off: Coupling, schema conflict. Shared read replica: Reporting simplicity — trade-off: Violates write ownership. Data warehouse ETL: Analytics separation — trade-off: Latency for operational reads.

Consistency Eventual + sagas common Local ACID

Part 1

Concept

Shared Database — Shared Database is an anti-pattern in microservices where multiple services read and write the same database schema, creating hidden coupling and deployment dependencies.

Teams choose shared databases for convenience — reporting joins, legacy migration, or avoiding distributed transactions. The result: schema changes require multi-team coordination, one service's slow query impacts all, and independent deployability becomes fiction.

Mental Model

[Order Svc] ----\
                 +--> [ SHARED PostgreSQL ]
[Payment Svc] --/         orders | payments | inventory
[Report Svc] ---/          (everyone reads/writes)

Key Terms

Term Definition
Integration database DB used as integration point between services.
Schema coupling Multiple services depend on same table structure.
Distributed monolith Separate deployables sharing one brain.
Lock contention Concurrent writers on shared tables.
Migration coordination Flyway/Liquibase conflicts across teams.

Why Architects Care

  • Shared Database shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How Shared Database evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
2000s Shared DB in 3-tier apps Normal for monoliths
2014 Microservices movement Shared DB labeled anti-pattern
2017 Strangler migrations Legacy DB shared during transition
2020 Database-as-integration smell Industry consensus against
2024 Modular monolith shared DB OK Context-dependent acceptance

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt Shared Database because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: Why do microservices with separate codebases still deploy together and fail together?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. Schema migration requires global release freeze
  2. No single team owns data invariants
  3. Performance debugging impossible — who caused the slow query?
  4. Security: over-privileged DB credentials across services
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

When services share a database, they share schema contracts, migration timing, connection pools, and failure modes. A column rename in one team's service breaks another's deploy — the worst of distributed and monolithic worlds.

Design Goals

Goal How Shared Database Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for Shared Database follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

[Order Svc] ----\
                 +--> [ SHARED PostgreSQL ]
[Payment Svc] --/         orders | payments | inventory
[Report Svc] ---/          (everyone reads/writes)

Step-by-Step

  1. Service A writes to shared orders table
  2. Service B reads same table directly (bypassing A's API)
  3. Team A migrates schema — Team B's deploy breaks
  4. Long-running report locks rows affecting OLTP
  5. No clear owner for table invariants

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges
Part 6

Failure Modes

When Shared Database is misapplied, these failures appear repeatedly:

  • Schema migration requires global release freeze
  • No single team owns data invariants
  • Performance debugging impossible — who caused the slow query?
  • Security: over-privileged DB credentials across services

Incident Pattern

User request ──► missing timeout ──► thread pool exhaustion ──► cascading 503s
                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges
Part 7

Scale Considerations

Shared Database at Amazon/Netflix/Uber scale requires explicit capacity thinking:

  • Strangler fig keeps shared DB temporarily then splits
  • Views and ACL schemas as interim step
  • CDC to warehouse removes reporting excuse

Scale Checklist

Dimension Question to Answer
Throughput What RPS per instance before saturation?
Data growth Which store becomes the bottleneck first?
Fan-out How many downstream calls per request?
Multi-region What consistency trade-off is acceptable?
Part 8

Performance

Performance for Shared Database is dominated by integration cost, not local CPU:

  • Shared connection pool max connections hit faster
  • Index changes affect all consumers unpredictably
  • Hot row updates serialize unrelated services
Factor Typical Impact Mitigation
Network hops +1–5 ms per sync call Cache, batch, async where safe
Serialization CPU on large payloads Schema evolution, compression
Connection pools Queueing under burst Pool sizing + backpressure

Part 1

Concept

REST Fundamentals — REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems using stateless HTTP operations on resources identified by URIs.

Roy Fielding defined REST in his 2000 dissertation. Resources (orders, users) are manipulated via HTTP verbs: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove). Representations (JSON, XML) transfer state. Stateless servers enable horizontal scaling.

Mental Model

Client --GET /orders/42--> Server
Client <--200 JSON {id:42, status:"SHIPPED"}-- Server

Key Terms

Term Definition
Resource Domain object identified by URI (/orders/123).
Representation JSON/XML encoding of resource state.
Stateless Each request contains all context; no server session.
Uniform interface Standard HTTP verbs and status codes.
HATEOAS Hypermedia links guide client navigation.

Why Architects Care

  • REST Fundamentals shapes how teams divide ownership, deploy independently, and recover from failure.
  • The pattern is not academic — it appears in production incident postmortems and hiring loops.
  • Senior engineers explain both the business driver and the runtime mechanism behind the name.
Part 2

History

How REST Fundamentals evolved in industry practice:

Era Dominant Practice What Changed
2000 Fielding REST dissertation Architectural constraints defined
2004 Amazon REST APIs Pragmatic JSON adoption
2010 Richardson Maturity Model Levels 0-3 for REST adoption
2015 OpenAPI standardization Contract-first REST
2020 REST + GraphQL coexistence REST for CRUD, GraphQL for aggregation

Historical Lesson

Industry did not adopt REST Fundamentals because of hype — each shift solved a measurable pain: release cadence, team autonomy, operational cost, or regulatory isolation. Understanding the era helps you avoid reintroducing old problems under new labels.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problem: How do clients interact with server resources over HTTP in a consistent, scalable way?

Symptoms in Production

Symptom Likely Root Cause
Slow releases Tight coupling blocks independent deploys
Blast radius grows Shared runtime or database without boundaries
On-call fatigue Hidden dependencies between components
Scaling cost spikes Monolithic scaling pays for unused capacity

Failure Modes

  1. Verbs misused — GET with side effects
  2. No proper status codes — always 200
  3. Session state on server breaking scale
  4. RPC disguised as REST (/orders/create)
Part 4

Why This Pattern Exists

Ad-hoc RPC-over-HTTP endpoints (/doOrder, /getUser) lack predictability. REST's uniform interface lets clients and intermediaries (caches, proxies) behave consistently.

Design Goals

Goal How REST Fundamentals Helps
Change isolation Teams evolve parts without freezing the whole system
Operational clarity Boundaries expose where latency, errors, and data live
Replaceability Implementations swap behind stable contracts
Testability Smaller surfaces enable focused integration tests
Part 5

Internal Working

Runtime behavior for REST Fundamentals follows a concrete sequence — not magic:

Internal Pipeline

Client --GET /orders/42--> Server
Client <--200 JSON {id:42, status:"SHIPPED"}-- Server

Step-by-Step

  1. Client sends HTTP request to resource URI
  2. Server authenticates and authorizes
  3. Handler maps verb+URI to domain operation
  4. Resource state serialized to representation
  5. HTTP status code and headers returned

Runtime Contracts

Contract Responsibility
API boundary Stable inputs/outputs across versions
Data ownership One writer per aggregate where possible
Failure propagation Timeouts and bulkheads at integration edges

                      │
                      └── fix: explicit budgets + circuit breakers at edges
